blocks.md: Many programs spend most of their time **waiting**: for the network, the disk, a timer, a user. A web server may hold ten thousand connections, each idle most of the time. One thread per connection works but is expensive (chapter 16: each thread has its own stack and costs the OS scheduler). **Async** lets one thread juggle many waiting tasks: whenever a task would wait, it steps aside and another runs.

blocks.title: Futures
blocks.md:
The core idea is the **future**: a value that may not be ready yet, but will be at some point. In Rust a future is any type implementing the **`Future`** trait. You rarely write one by hand; instead:

- **`async fn`** declares a function that returns a future instead of running its body immediately.
- **`.await`** inside an async function or block waits for a future to finish and gives its result. While it waits, the task yields control so other work can run.

```rust
async fn page_title(url: &str) -> Option<String> {
    let response_text = trpl::get(url).await.text().await;
    Html::parse(&response_text)
        .select_first("title")
        .map(|title| title.inner_html())
}
```

This is *The Rust Programming Language*'s first async function. It reads like normal sequential code; the `await`s mark where it may pause. `.await` is a **postfix** keyword, so calls chain naturally.

blocks.title: async fn returns a future
blocks.md: The compiler rewrites `async fn page_title(url: &str) -> Option<String>` into roughly `fn page_title(url: &str) -> impl Future<Output = Option<String>>`. The body becomes a **state machine**: one state per `.await` point, storing the local variables that must survive the pause. No extra thread, no heap allocation unless you ask for one.

blocks.title: Futures are lazy
blocks.md: Like iterators, futures do nothing until something drives them. Calling an `async fn` only **creates** the future. Something must **poll** it repeatedly until it is done; `.await` does that from inside other async code. The compiler warns when you create one and drop it:

blocks.explain: This prints only `start`. The future returned by `say_hello()` is created and immediately dropped, never polled.

warning: unused implementer of `Future` that must be used

7 |     say_hello();

  = note: futures do nothing unless you `.await` or poll them

blocks.title: Runtimes and executors
Building block_on yourself
blocks.md:
An executor is less magic than it sounds. *Programming Rust* builds one in a dozen lines, and you can too, with only the standard library. You need two facts, explained fully in lesson 3:

1. Polling a future returns `Poll::Ready(value)` or `Poll::Pending`.
2. A pending future arranges to be **woken** when it can make progress, through a **`Waker`** it gets from the executor.

So `block_on` polls; on `Pending` it puts the thread to sleep with `thread::park()`; the waker's job is to `unpark` it.

blocks.explain: `pin!` fixes the future in place on the stack; lesson 3 explains why futures must not move once polled. `Wake` is a standard trait that turns any `Arc<T: Wake>` into a `Waker`. Real executors add a task queue and I/O integration, but the loop is the same.

blocks.title: async blocks and move
blocks.md: Besides `async fn`, an **`async` block** creates a future in place: `let fut = async { ... };`. Like closures, async blocks capture variables from their surroundings by reference, unless written **`async move`**, which takes ownership. You need `async move` when the future outlives the current scope, for example when it is handed to another task.

blocks.output:
Hello, Ferris! Hello, Corro!
names still here: 2
blocks.explain: The outer block borrows `names`, which is fine because `block_on` finishes before `main` continues. `make_greeting` must use `async move`: the future it returns outlives the function's parameter.

blocks.title: Count the polls
blocks.md: `YieldOnce` is a future that returns `Pending` the first time it is polled (waking itself immediately) and `Ready` the second time. Add a counter to `block_on` so it returns how many times it polled, and print it. Awaiting three `YieldOnce`s in a row should need 4 polls of the outer future: one per pause, plus the final one.
hints: `let mut polls = 0;` before the loop, `polls += 1;` before each `poll`, and `return (v, polls)`.
`wake_by_ref` unparks the thread before it parks, so `park` returns at once: a parked thread with a pending unpark token wakes immediately.

points: Async gives concurrency for waiting-heavy work without a thread per task.
A future is a value that will be ready later; `async fn` returns one and `.await` waits for it.
Futures are lazy: nothing happens until an executor polls them.
Runtimes such as Tokio provide executors and async I/O; the standard library provides only the traits.
`block_on` is a loop: poll, and on `Pending` park until the `Waker` unparks.

terms.def: A value implementing Future that represents a computation which may complete later.
A function whose body runs as a future; calling it returns the future.
A postfix operator that waits for a future, letting other tasks run in the meantime.
A library that executes futures and provides async I/O, timers and channels, such as Tokio.
The part of a runtime that polls futures until they complete.
Several tasks making progress in overlapping periods of time.
Several tasks running at the same instant on different processors.
